output.observation: mart_rows=267, dim_rows=400, ci_matched_customers=400, missing_from_mart_but_recoverable_ci=133, missing_and_truly_absent=0. All 400 customers match case-insensitively; none of the 133 missing customers are actually gone from the source.

output.narrative: customer_enrichment is a view whose row count is governed by an INNER JOIN of customers_dim to orders_current on customer_code (e16, e1). It emits only 267 of 400 customers, silently dropping 133, even though orders_current carries a distinct code for all 400 with zero NULL/blank values — a join-match failure, not missing data (e2). The 133 dropped customers are stored in customers_dim in lowercase (cust-0003, cust-0006, … every third code) while orders_current holds the identical codes in uppercase (CUST-0003, …), and matched customers are uppercase in both tables (e3, e14). A case-sensitive join matches 267 while a case-insensitive (UPPER) join matches all 400, recovering every one of the 133 lowercase codes — no customer or order is actually gone (e4, e24). The trigger is in-window migration M-0042 (day 16), which set customers_dim.customer_code to the case-sensitive collation utf8mb4_0900_as_cs, turning the previously case-insensitive join comparison case-sensitive (e5). No input arrived corrupted: the keys are well-formed and differ only by case (e22), and all 133 missing customers still exist in customers_dim with a case-insensitive match in orders_current (e11). Nobody intended the join to drop these rows — the measurement's comparison rule broke.
